editorial_note: GitHub listed sixteen projects this Thursday morning. NVIDIA's Auto Ontology tops both the list and our picks: ==a semantic layer that makes data agents show their work==. Spec Kit and PR-Agent cover the coding workflow from spec to review, agent-desktop returns because its new release adds an MCP server, and kimi-k3-in-c runs a 2.78-trillion-parameter model from disk on one CPU, slowly. Disc Image Studio is the day's pure delight, and Horizon builds a personal AI news briefing. Curation order reflects practical interest, not GitHub rank. Trending is not a release date or an endorsement.
coverage_notes: All 16 listing entries were inspected. Exact public GitHub API metadata was checked for the ten entries never featured before and for vercel-labs/agent-desktop at about 07:01 UTC, recent releases for 13 entries, and README files for eleven; every checked repository was active and unarchived. All seven picks have a licence detected by GitHub's API (Apache-2.0, MIT or GPL-3.0).
One repeat: vercel-labs/agent-desktop (3 November), because v1.2.0, published at 02:43 UTC today, adds an MCP server; the change is described on its card.

Five entries featured before were left out without a material change: max-sixty/worktrunk and D4Vinci/Scrapling (3 November), floci-io/floci (4 November), thedotmack/claude-mem (30 October and 2 November) and mattpocock/skills (31 October). Worktrunk, Floci and mattpocock/skills have had no release since; claude-mem's v15.9.0 was already noted on 3 November; Scrapling's v0.5.1 (4 November evening) adds agent drag-and-drop and remote browser sessions but was judged an incremental follow-up to the v0.5 covered then.

New entries not picked: harry0703/MoneyPrinterTurbo (an established automatic short-video generator whose README leads with model-API sponsor offers), garrytan/gstack (a personal Claude Code skill set close to setups covered before), scenario-labs/skills (agent skills that mostly need a Scenario account) and MichaelCade/90DaysOfDevOps (a DevOps learning path last updated in June, whose licence GitHub's API reports as Other).
No security-focused project was on today's list.
The preceding seven calendar dates, 29 October-4 November, were checked for local history; all seven editions exist.

The official listing was captured at 08:00:42 Europe/Paris. Literal stars-today labels are GitHub's displayed period figures; API total stars and README evidence were checked separately at the times shown per card. They are not an independently audited rolling 24-hour growth measurement.

Feature, speed and quality descriptions are the maintainers' own, including kimi-k3-in-c's memory and per-token timings, PR-Agent's single-call claim and Disc Image Studio's sample results. No candidate code, installer, extension, checkpoint or model was installed, downloaded or run, and none of this is a security audit or endorsement.

projects.description: An ==open library from NVIDIA that builds a semantic layer== over company databases so AI agents can answer data questions reliably. It generates an ontology (business terms, metrics, relationships and lineage) from existing metadata, reconciles conflicting definitions across systems, turns natural-language questions into SQL, and serves that context to agents over MCP, a CLI and an API. It ships a web UI, Postgres with pgvector, and Docker Compose or Helm deployment.
projects.why_interesting: First time on our list, and first on today's. Text-to-SQL agents often fail on meaning rather than syntax: which revenue column is the certified one. Auto Ontology's answer is to ==check generated queries against certified definitions and return provenance==, the SQL and the steps behind every answer, so a person can audit the number. It is Apache-2.0 and comes from NVIDIA's own GitHub organization.
projects.caveat: The default setup ==depends on NVIDIA NIM model endpoints and an NVIDIA API key== (hosted or self-hosted), plus Docker, Postgres and optionally HashiCorp Vault for database credentials. An agent connected to databases runs queries with those permissions, so use read-only accounts. The README says the project ==does not accept external contributions==, and it has no tagged release yet. Benchmark results live in a separate evaluation repository. We did not run it.

projects.description: GitHub's ==toolkit that gives AI coding agents structured processes==. A Specify CLI sets up a project, and agent commands carry a feature from a written specification through plan, tasks and implementation. Bundled extensions add bug fixing (assessed cause, scoped fix, recorded verification) and idea assessment (go, clarify or stop), while presets, workflows and catalogs let teams adapt or share their own process. It works with Copilot and many other coding agents.
projects.why_interesting: First time on our list. Spec-driven development is a counterweight to vibe coding: ==the spec and plan become reviewable files==, so a team can check intent before code exists. It is an official GitHub project under MIT and moving fast: v1.3.0 (3 November) moved the core issue-export command into a separate github extension and fixed several workflow and extension bugs.
projects.caveat: It adds process and files to every feature, which ==can be overkill for small changes==. Community catalog components are third-party code, and the README itself says listings are not audits, so review their source before installing. Frequent releases include breaking changes such as v1.3.0's removal, so pin a version. Results still depend on the coding agent you connect. We did not install it.

projects.description: An ==open-source AI pull-request reviewer== that runs as a GitHub Action, a webhook service, a Docker image or a CLI. Commands such as /describe, /review, /improve and /ask post a PR description, review comments, suggested changes or answers. It supports GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Azure DevOps and Gitea, and any model reachable through LiteLLM, including local models via Ollama.
projects.why_interesting: First time on our list. It is the original Qodo PR-Agent, ==now donated to a community-owned organization== with an external maintainer, which makes it a self-hostable alternative to paid review bots: your diff goes only to the model provider you choose. The README says each tool uses a single model call; v0.49.0 (25 October) added a pr-agent doctor preflight, JSON output and security hardening.
projects.caveat: Review quality and cost depend on the model you pay for, and your diffs are sent to that provider. The /help_docs tool ==has been disabled since v0.36.1 pending a credential-exposure fix==, and v0.49.0 changed several defaults (GitHub polling allowlist, Jira project scope, default model), so read the upgrade notes before updating. It is distinct from Qodo's hosted product. We did not run it.

projects.description: A ==command-line tool that lets AI agents operate desktop apps== on macOS, Windows and Linux through the operating system's accessibility tree. An agent takes a JSON snapshot with a reference for each element, acts on a reference, then snapshots again to check the result, with no screenshot pixel matching.
projects.why_interesting: Repeat from 3 November, for a material change: ==v1.2.0, published this morning, adds an MCP server==. The agent-desktop mcp command serves every command as an MCP tool over stdio, so MCP-capable agents can use it without shell wrappers. The release also fixes macOS list-row selection and draws the cursor overlay above menus. It drew the most stars of anything on today's list.
projects.caveat: An easier hookup also makes it easier to ==hand an agent control of every open app== your account can reach, so keep tasks narrow and treat on-screen text as untrusted input. The README warns that snapshots, clipboard reads and screenshots can contain private desktop content. The project is barely a week past v1.0.0, and the MCP server is one day old. We did not install it.

projects.description: A ==small, dependency-free C99 inference engine for Moonshot AI's Kimi K3==, a 2.78-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts model. Instead of holding the model in memory, it streams the 1.56 TB checkpoint from disk on each step, so it runs on one CPU with no GPU, BLAS or framework; more RAM only makes it faster. It builds on Linux, macOS and Windows, and its README is a long walkthrough of how each part works.
projects.why_interesting: First time on our list. It is a ==readable demonstration that RAM need not be the hard limit== for running a frontier-size open model: the README reports a peak of 8.24 GB of memory, byte-identical output across machine sizes, and a test suite that runs in about a minute without the checkpoint. Even if you never run the full model, the code and write-up are a tour of mixture-of-experts inference.
projects.caveat: It is ==very slow by design==: the README's own figures are roughly 20 to 33 seconds per token below 128 GB of RAM and 5.6 seconds above, measured on a fast NVMe machine. Running it ==needs about 1.7 TB of free disk==, a Hugging Face token to download the weights, and acceptance of Moonshot AI's model license; the Apache-2.0 license covers only this code. All figures are the author's. We downloaded and ran nothing.

projects.description: A ==tool that burns a visible picture onto an ordinary optical disc==. It converts an image into data laid out to match the physical tracks of a CD, DVD or single-layer BD-R, so a normal burner writes a pattern you can see by eye on the recording surface. It has a layer-based designer, dithering and tone controls, disc-brand presets, photo-based calibration of track geometry, and exports ISO, RAW or WAV+CUE images or burns directly.
projects.why_interesting: First time on our list. It is ==a clever hardware hack with no special drive or disc==: the README says any burner and blank disc work, and its calibration step, photographing a test burn to fit the disc's radii and track pitch, is documented with before-and-after photos. It is GPL-licensed, documented in seven languages and actively developed, with releases on 4 and 5 November.
projects.caveat: The full desktop app is ==Windows-only; Linux and macOS get an experimental command-line version==. Direct streaming burn is experimental, the README says to use only blank, expendable test discs, and the Windows release EXE is unsigned. The latest release notes say a readback problem (issue 90) is not yet confirmed fixed. Results depend on media and drive, and the sample photos are the author's. We did not run it.

projects.description: A ==self-hosted, AI-powered news briefing generator==. It collects items from RSS, Hacker News, Reddit, Telegram channels, X, GitHub and financial news, scores and deduplicates them with a language model according to per-topic profiles, adds web-researched background and community discussion, and publishes a daily briefing in English and Chinese as Markdown, a GitHub Pages site, email, webhooks or WeChat.
projects.why_interesting: First time on our list. Its profiles make the editorial rules explicit and editable: ==each kind of content gets its own scoring rubric and output== (impact for news, practical takeaways for engineering blogs), with caps so one busy topic cannot crowd out the rest. It runs from a CLI, from an AI assistant over MCP or as an agent skill, and works with Claude, GPT, Gemini, DeepSeek or local Ollama models. MIT-licensed.
projects.caveat: Every run ==spends model API calls==, and cost grows with the number of sources and the enrichment you enable. The X source goes through Apify, a paid third-party scraping service, and scraping can conflict with a site's terms. Model-written summaries can be wrong, so keep the links to the originals. There is no tagged release. We did not run it.
